Line 1 | TW-WL-H01-L1 | XIANG-U-01-02

001爻 Historical event Cincinnatus returns to his farm. Rome faced a military emergency and appointed Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus dictator, an extraordinary office with broad authority. Ancient tradition presents him as a landowner who had been away from ordinary public office when the summons came. He accepted the appointment, organized the Roman response, and after the emergency relinquished the dictatorship rather than keeping exceptional power. He then returned to private life and agricultural work. The episode was later retold as an example of temporary service rather than permanent possession of office. The historical details come through later Roman writers and should not be treated as a complete contemporary record. Even so, the sequence is clear in the tradition: urgent public duty interrupted private work, the task was completed, and the office was surrendered. His return to the farm became part of his long afterlife in European and American civic culture. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The record does not require invented dialogue or private motives to make the decision understandable. It can be followed through observable actions, roles, projects, and later consequences. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. What matters historically is the chain from the conditions before the choice, through the work required to carry it out, to the consequences that became visible afterward. Later reputation can make the result look obvious, but it was not obvious at the beginning. The value of the episode lies in the documented sequence of action and consequence, not in turning the person into a flawless model.

Line-specific comparison The hidden dragon places capability below public authority. For a workplace or life decision, this line is useful before the visible move begins. Set beside Cincinnatus returns to his farm, the image becomes concrete rather than abstract. Cincinnatus returns to his farm. Rome faced a military emergency and appointed Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus dictator, an extraordinary office with broad authority.. The decision changed duties, relationships, resources, or the direction of work; it did not guarantee an easy outcome. Creative capacity matters, but finishing a demanding assignment can include knowing when to release authority and return to ordinary life. The case of Cincinnatus returns. For this line, timing, fit, responsibility, restraint, or follow-through should be judged at the stage represented here, not from the final result alone. Later reputation can make the result look obvious, but it was not obvious at the beginning. The value of the episode lies in the documented. What must exist before a professional claim becomes credible? This is a present-day editorial comparison. Historical case EUUS-WL-H02: Augustine leaves a rhetoric career · Milan and North Africa, Europe · 386–391 CE

Line 1 | TW-WL-H02-L1 | XIANG-U-02-02▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H02-L1 | XIANG-U-02-02

007爻 Historical event Augustine leaves a rhetoric career. Augustine had built a career as a teacher of rhetoric and eventually held a prestigious teaching post in Milan. His work depended on education, public speaking, and the patronage networks of the late Roman world. During the 380s he withdrew from that professional path, was baptized in Milan in 387, and returned to North Africa. He formed a religious community, was ordained a priest at Hippo, and later became bishop. The transition replaced a career centered on rhetoric with one centered on pastoral, intellectual, and institutional work. He continued writing and teaching for decades, but within a different vocation and set of responsibilities. His later books drew on skills developed in his earlier education while serving a new audience and purpose. The decision did not erase the first career; it redirected capabilities acquired there into a different form of work and life. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The record does not require invented dialogue or private motives to make the decision understandable. It can be followed through observable actions, roles, projects, and later consequences. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. What matters historically is the chain from the conditions before the choice, through the work required to carry it out, to the consequences that became visible afterward. Later reputation can make the result look obvious, but it was not obvious at the beginning. The value of the episode lies in the documented sequence of action and consequence, not in turning the person into a flawless model.

He established a monastery at Monte Cassino and is associated with the Rule of Saint Benedict, which organized prayer, reading, manual labor, obedience, hospitality, and community life. The rule treated daily work as part of a disciplined common rhythm rather than as an activity separate from spiritual life. Benedictine communities later spread across Europe and adapted the rule to different places and centuries. The monastery became not simply a retreat but a durable institution with roles, schedules, shared resources, and procedures for leadership. 019爻 Historical event Hildegard founds Rupertsberg. Hildegard of Bingen became a leader within a religious community at Disibodenberg, where women lived under arrangements connected to a male monastery. As her community and reputation grew, the existing setting no longer matched all of its needs. She pursued the creation of a separate convent at Rupertsberg near Bingen. The move required ecclesiastical approval, property, construction, funding, and the transfer of a community. From the new base she managed correspondence, music, writing, religious duties, and relationships with patrons and church authorities. Rupertsberg became the center of her later work, and she eventually founded another house at Eibingen. The change illustrates a practical workplace decision inside a medieval institution: seeking a structure with greater operational independence while retaining obligations to a wider network. The result was not immediate freedom from constraint, but a new platform for sustained work. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. 025爻 Historical event Gutenberg builds a printing enterprise. Johannes Gutenberg worked in a world where books were copied by hand or produced with labor-intensive methods. His printing project required more than one invention: movable metal type, ink, presses, skilled labor, paper, and substantial financing had to work together. In Mainz he entered financial arrangements with Johann Fust and developed a workshop capable of producing large printed works, including the Bible associated with his name. The enterprise required repeated experiments and expensive equipment before revenue could be realized. A later legal dispute with Fust affected control of the workshop and its assets. Printing nevertheless spread rapidly through European cities after the 1450s. Gutenberg did not personally control the entire industry that followed, but the system demonstrated that standardized text production could be organized as a repeatable business process. The case is a reminder that waiting during development can be active work when the product requires integration before launch. 031爻 Historical event Michelangelo accepts the Sistine ceiling commission. Michelangelo was known primarily as a sculptor when Pope Julius II commissioned him to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. The assignment was large, technically difficult, and outside the medium for which he had built his strongest reputation. He accepted the work and organized scaffolding, assistants, materials, and fresco production over several years. He revised the working process as the project developed and completed a vast sequence of figures across the ceiling. The commission interrupted other work and placed him inside a demanding patron relationship. The finished ceiling became one of the best-known works of Renaissance art and altered Michelangelo’s professional identity, making painting a central part of how later audiences understood him. The episode was not free of disagreement or pressure, but it shows a career decision in which conflict with role expectations did not prevent a person from completing work beyond the boundaries of an earlier specialty. Line 1 | TW-WL-H07-L1 | XIANG-U-07-02

037爻 Historical event Leonardo moves to Milan. Leonardo da Vinci trained and worked in Florence, but opportunities there were shared among many established artists and workshops. In the early 1480s he moved to Milan and entered the service of Ludovico Sforza. His work in Milan extended beyond painting. He designed court entertainments, studied engineering and anatomy, proposed military devices, and worked on projects including The Last Supper and a large equestrian monument that was never completed. Service at court required him to combine artistic ability with technical, organizational, and representational tasks. The Milan period lasted many years and broadened the range of Leonardo’s professional practice. Political change later forced him to leave, showing that a career built around a patron could also be vulnerable to the patron’s circumstances. The move nevertheless demonstrates how a deliberate change of environment can expand the range of work available to a skilled person. Historical case EUUS-WL-H08: Boulton and Watt form a partnership · Birmingham, Britain · 1775

Line 1 | TW-WL-H08-L1 | XIANG-U-08-02▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H08-L1 | XIANG-U-08-02

043爻 Historical event Boulton and Watt form a partnership. James Watt had developed improvements to the steam engine but faced the usual difficulties of turning an invention into a reliable commercial product. Building engines required capital, manufacturing capability, customers, installation, and maintenance. Matthew Boulton brought an established manufacturing base at Soho and experience in business organization. Their partnership combined Watt’s engineering work with Boulton’s production resources and commercial network. They licensed and supplied engines for mines and factories while continuing to improve designs and manage technical problems in the field. The partnership became one of the best-known industrial collaborations of the eighteenth century. Its success depended less on a single inspired moment than on complementary roles maintained over time. 049爻 Historical event Benjamin Franklin establishes himself as a printer. Benjamin Franklin left his apprenticeship in Boston as a young man and arrived in Philadelphia with limited resources. Printing was a skilled trade that required equipment, customers, credit, and reputation, none of which could be created instantly. He worked for other printers, traveled to London, returned to Philadelphia, and eventually entered business on his own. He built a printing shop, published the Pennsylvania Gazette, produced Poor Richard’s Almanack, and developed relationships through civic and commercial activity. The growth was incremental and depended on repeated small decisions about work, saving, partnerships, and public reliability. The printing business gave Franklin financial independence and a platform for later scientific and civic work. His path was not a straight promotion inside one employer; it was a sequence of apprenticeships, moves, experiments, and accumulated credibility. The case shows how modest gains can compound before a career appears established from the outside. 054爻 Historical event Benjamin Franklin establishes himself as a printer. Benjamin Franklin left his apprenticeship in Boston as a young man and arrived in Philadelphia with limited resources. Printing was a skilled trade that required equipment, customers, credit, and reputation, none of which could be created instantly. He worked for other printers, traveled to London, returned to Philadelphia, and eventually entered business on his own. He built a printing shop, published the Pennsylvania Gazette, produced Poor Richard’s Almanack, and developed relationships through civic and commercial activity. The growth was incremental and depended on repeated small decisions about work, saving, partnerships, and public reliability. The printing business gave Franklin financial independence and a platform for later scientific and civic work. His path was not a straight promotion inside one employer; it was a sequence of apprenticeships, moves, experiments, and accumulated credibility. The case shows how modest gains can compound before a career appears established from the outside. 055爻 Historical event Charles Darwin accepts the Beagle voyage. After university, Charles Darwin had not settled into a conventional profession. An opportunity arose to join HMS Beagle as a gentleman companion and naturalist on a surveying voyage, but the journey promised years away from home and no guaranteed career outcome. Darwin accepted after family discussion and sailed in 1831. During the voyage he collected specimens, recorded geological observations, corresponded with scientists, and encountered environments across South America and the Pacific. The work required careful routines of note-taking, preservation, comparison, and shipment back to Britain. When he returned in 1836, the collections and observations helped establish his scientific reputation. Years of further research followed before he published On the Origin of Species in 1859. The initial decision did not produce an immediate breakthrough; it placed him on a path where disciplined observation created options that had not existed before the voyage. 061爻 Historical event Bell Labs organizes the transistor team. Telephone networks needed more reliable and efficient electronic components than vacuum tubes could provide for many applications. Bell Labs had the resources to pursue fundamental physics and practical engineering in the same organization. A team including John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley worked on semiconductor problems. In 1947 Bardeen and Brattain demonstrated a working point-contact transistor, while Shockley later developed the junction transistor concept. The work involved theory, experiments, measurement, fabrication, and institutional support rather than a solitary invention. The transistor became a foundational technology for modern electronics. The individual relationships within the team later became strained, but the initial research environment demonstrated the value of assembling complementary expertise around a shared technical problem. Progress came from interaction among roles that could not be collapsed into one job description. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. 067爻 Historical event Kodak develops but delays digital photography. Eastman Kodak dominated film photography when engineer Steven Sasson was asked to explore a new solid-state imaging technology. In 1975 he built an early self-contained digital camera prototype using a CCD sensor and digital storage. The prototype showed that photographs could be captured without film, but the image quality, speed, storage, and display ecosystem were still primitive. Kodak continued research and obtained important digital-imaging patents while its existing business remained tied to film, processing, and photographic paper. Over subsequent decades competitors and new consumer electronics companies advanced digital cameras and later camera phones. Kodak eventually sold digital products, but the transition undermined the economics of its historical core business. The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 2012 and later emerged as a smaller business. The case is useful as a workplace decision story because recognizing a new technology and reorganizing around it are different tasks. 073爻 Historical event Hewlett and Packard build a company partnership. Bill Hewlett and David Packard met as engineering students at Stanford and later explored the idea of building electronic instruments. They started a small business in a rented garage in Palo Alto in 1939. Their early work included an audio oscillator that found a customer in Walt Disney Studios. As the company grew, the founders developed management practices that emphasized technical competence, decentralized responsibility, and respect for employees. HP expanded from instruments into computing and other technologies over several decades. The company’s later history included major restructurings and splits, but its early partnership became an influential example of Silicon Valley company building. 079爻 Historical event Andrew Carnegie sells Carnegie Steel. Andrew Carnegie had built one of the largest steel businesses in the United States through investment in plants, technology, transportation, and aggressive cost control. By the end of the nineteenth century he was extremely wealthy and still associated with a demanding industrial enterprise. In 1901 J. P. Morgan organized the purchase of Carnegie Steel and combined it with other businesses to form U.S. Steel. Carnegie left active steel management with a fortune that made him one of the richest individuals of his era. He then devoted much of his remaining life to philanthropy, funding libraries, education, research, and foundations. The sale changed both his professional identity and the use of his resources. It did not erase controversies surrounding labor relations in the steel industry, including the Homestead conflict. As a life decision, the case shows that possessing more resources creates a second question: whether to keep maximizing the activity that created them or redirect them toward a different purpose. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. 085爻 Historical event George Washington Carver joins Tuskegee. George Washington Carver trained in agriculture and earned a graduate degree at Iowa State Agricultural College. In 1896 Booker T. Washington invited him to lead agricultural work at Tuskegee Institute in Alabama. Carver accepted and spent much of his career at Tuskegee, teaching, conducting experiments, and producing practical bulletins for farmers. His work emphasized crop rotation, soil improvement, and uses for crops such as peanuts and sweet potatoes. Facilities and resources were limited compared with major research institutions, so he often worked with modest equipment and materials. Carver became nationally known, although popular stories later exaggerated some claims about his inventions. 091爻 Historical event Walt Disney commits to Snow White. By the mid-1930s Walt Disney’s studio was successful with animated shorts, but a feature-length animated film had not yet been proven as a commercial format in Hollywood. Producing one would require years of work, new artistic methods, training, and large financial commitments. Disney committed the studio to Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs. Costs rose as the project expanded, and the company had to manage thousands of drawings, music, story development, effects, and production schedules. The film premiered in 1937 and was released widely in 1938. Its commercial success gave the studio resources and credibility for additional feature films and a larger production organization. The decision also increased the scale and complexity of the workplace. 103爻 Historical event IBM brings in Lou Gerstner. IBM entered the early 1990s under severe financial pressure as computing shifted away from the mainframe-centered environment in which the company had long been dominant. Losses, internal complexity, and fragmented product groups raised questions about whether IBM should be broken into separate companies. In 1993 the board hired Lou Gerstner, an outsider to the computer industry, as chief executive. He chose to keep the company together and emphasized integrated services, customer needs, cost reduction, and changes in internal culture. IBM reduced expenses and reorganized incentives while expanding its services business. The company returned to profitability and remained a large technology firm, although later decades brought new challenges. The turnaround did not restore the old world of computing; it repaired the organization so that it could compete in a different one. The workplace lesson is about treating institutional decay as a problem to diagnose and redesign rather than simply defend. IBM entered the early 1990s under severe financial pressure as computing shifted away from the mainframe-centered environment in which the company had long been dominant. Losses, internal complexity, and fragmented product groups raised questions about whether IBM should be broken into separate companies. In 1993 the board hired Lou Gerstner, an outsider to the computer industry, as chief executive. He chose to keep the company together and emphasized integrated services, customer needs, cost reduction, and changes in internal culture. IBM reduced expenses and reorganized incentives while expanding its services business. The company returned to profitability and remained a large technology firm, although later decades brought new challenges. The turnaround did not restore the old world of computing; it repaired the organization so that it could compete in a different one. The workplace lesson is about treating institutional decay as a problem to diagnose and redesign rather than simply defend. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. What matters historically is the chain from the conditions before the choice, through the work required to carry it out, to the consequences that became visible afterward. 109爻 Historical event Howard Schultz returns to Starbucks. Starbucks expanded rapidly during the 1990s and 2000s, but by the financial crisis the company faced slowing sales, store closures, and criticism that rapid growth had weakened parts of the customer experience. Howard Schultz had stepped away from the chief executive role while remaining chairman. He returned as CEO in 2008. Starbucks closed underperforming stores, slowed expansion, retrained baristas, and refocused on coffee quality, store experience, and digital loyalty programs. One highly publicized decision temporarily closed many U.S. stores for employee training. The company recovered and resumed growth, though it continued to face labor, market, and competitive issues in later years. The case shows the decision to approach a struggling organization directly rather than manage it only through financial targets. Returning leadership mattered because it was paired with operational changes visible to employees and customers. 115爻 Historical event Peter Drucker chooses an independent knowledge-work career. Peter Drucker worked in banking, journalism, research, teaching, and consulting across Europe and the United States. Rather than building a conventional executive career inside one corporation, he developed a professional life around studying how organizations worked. His writing on General Motors and later books on management, knowledge work, objectives, nonprofit organizations, and executive effectiveness reached managers across industries. He taught for many years while continuing to advise organizations and write for broad audiences. The combination allowed ideas from one setting to be tested against another rather than remaining inside a single employer. Drucker became one of the most influential management writers of the twentieth century. His career illustrates a decision to make observation itself a form of work: stepping outside one organization sufficiently to compare many organizations, while remaining close enough to practice to ask operational questions. 121爻 Historical event Frances Perkins accepts the labor secretary role. Frances Perkins had spent years working on labor, workplace safety, and social reform in New York. The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire of 1911 became part of the context in which reformers pushed for stronger workplace protections. In 1933 President Franklin D. Roosevelt appointed Perkins Secretary of Labor, making her the first woman to serve in a U.S. presidential cabinet. She entered national office during the Great Depression and worked on employment policy, labor standards, and the development of Social Security legislation. Perkins served for twelve years and helped shape institutions that outlasted the immediate crisis. The role required moving from advocacy and state-level administration into a federal workplace where negotiation, legislation, bureaucracy, and political opposition were unavoidable. The career decision expanded her influence but also increased the scale of accountability. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. 127爻 Historical event Coco Chanel reopens her fashion house. Coco Chanel had closed her couture house during the Second World War and spent years outside the active Paris fashion business. By the early 1950s the industry had changed, and Christian Dior’s highly structured postwar styles dominated attention. In 1954, in her seventies, Chanel reopened her couture house and presented new collections based on the simpler lines, jersey, suits, and practical movement long associated with her work. French reviews were initially mixed, while American buyers and press were more receptive. The business gradually regained influence. Chanel’s return extended her career and helped establish styles that remained central to the brand after her death. The case is a workplace decision about re-entry: returning after a long absence without simply reproducing the old market. Presentation mattered, but the comeback depended on whether the product still solved practical needs for customers. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The record does not require invented dialogue or private motives to make the decision understandable. It can be followed through observable actions, roles, projects, and later consequences. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. What matters historically is the chain from the conditions before the choice, through the work required to carry it out, to the consequences that became visible afterward. Later reputation can make the result look obvious, but it was not obvious at the beginning. The value of the episode lies in the documented sequence of action and consequence, not in turning the person into a flawless model.

133爻 Historical event Kodak employee Steven Sasson presents the digital camera. Steven Sasson was a young electrical engineer at Eastman Kodak when he received an assignment to explore charge-coupled device imaging. Film remained central to the company’s revenues and identity. Sasson and colleagues assembled a prototype camera from available components. It recorded a low-resolution black-and-white image to a digital cassette and displayed it through separate equipment. He demonstrated the concept internally, where the idea raised practical questions about image quality, infrastructure, and how a filmless system might fit the company’s existing business. Kodak continued digital research and patented important technology, yet the eventual market transition proved disruptive. Sasson’s prototype later became recognized as an early milestone in digital photography. At the individual workplace level, the episode shows what can happen when an employee completes an assignment that challenges the assumptions of the organization that commissioned it. Line 1 | TW-WL-H25-L1 | XIANG-U-25-02

145爻 Historical event Alexander Fleming follows an unexpected laboratory observation. Alexander Fleming was researching bacteria at St Mary’s Hospital in London when he noticed that a mold contaminating a culture plate was associated with an area where bacteria did not grow normally. Laboratory contamination usually meant an experiment had failed. Instead of discarding the observation, Fleming investigated the mold and described the antibacterial substance he called penicillin. His early work did not produce a practical mass-produced drug. More than a decade later, researchers including Howard Florey, Ernst Chain, and their teams developed methods for purification, testing, and production, with wartime manufacturing expanding supply. Penicillin transformed treatment of bacterial infections and earned Fleming, Florey, and Chain the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The case is not a story of luck alone. An unexpected result created value because someone treated it as evidence worth examining rather than as noise to remove. 151爻 Historical event Warren Buffett closes his investment partnership. Warren Buffett had managed investment partnerships through the 1950s and 1960s using a value-oriented approach. By the late 1960s he judged the market environment less attractive for the methods and opportunities he had relied upon. In 1969 he dissolved the partnerships rather than continue simply because the structure had been successful. Investors received cash and securities, including interests connected with Berkshire Hathaway. Buffett then concentrated more heavily on Berkshire as a vehicle for owning businesses and investments over long periods. Berkshire later became a large conglomerate and investment company. The decision to stop one successful arrangement before beginning another is useful in a workplace and life context because it shows accumulation paired with restraint. 157爻 Historical event Alice Waters opens Chez Panisse. Alice Waters had studied in France and developed an interest in food shaped by fresh ingredients and shared meals. She did not begin with a conventional career path as a trained restaurant chef or hospitality executive. In 1971 she and collaborators opened Chez Panisse in Berkeley. The restaurant gradually built relationships with local farmers and suppliers and emphasized seasonal ingredients and simple preparation. Operations changed over time as the team learned how to run a restaurant, source consistent produce, and translate ideals about food into daily service. Chez Panisse became influential in American cooking and in discussions of local agriculture, school food, and sustainable sourcing. The work shows nourishment as an operational decision: values about health, quality, and community become meaningful only when purchasing, menus, schedules, and supplier relationships support them every day. Line 1 | TW-WL-H28-L1 | XIANG-U-28-02

163爻 Historical event NASA flight controllers manage Apollo 13. Apollo 13 launched in April 1970 as a planned lunar-landing mission. An oxygen tank explosion crippled the spacecraft on the way to the Moon, damaging electrical and life-support systems and ending the landing objective. Astronauts and NASA teams in Mission Control shifted immediately from exploration to survival. They used the lunar module as a lifeboat, conserved power and water, revised navigation procedures, and developed a method for adapting carbon-dioxide filters with materials available onboard. Engineers tested procedures on the ground before sending instructions to the crew. The astronauts returned safely to Earth. The mission was later studied as an example of crisis management, technical teamwork, and decision-making under constrained resources. The case shows a structure under excessive load: success came not from insisting on the original goal, but from redefining the goal and reducing demands to what the damaged system could still support. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. 175爻 Historical event Julia Child retrains in French cooking. Julia Child moved to France after the Second World War because of her husband Paul Child’s diplomatic posting. She had worked in wartime government service but had not established a professional career in food. In Paris she studied at Le Cordon Bleu, practiced intensively, and later collaborated with Simone Beck and Louisette Bertholle on a French cookbook for American readers. The manuscript went through years of testing, revision, and publishing difficulty before Mastering the Art of French Cooking appeared in 1961. Child then moved into television, where she demonstrated techniques for a mass audience. Her second career became highly influential in American food culture. The transition was gradual and collaborative rather than a single act of reinvention. It shows influence growing through shared work, repeated practice, and the ability to translate expertise from one culture and professional setting into another. In Paris she studied at Le Cordon Bleu, practiced intensively, and later collaborated with Simone Beck and Louisette Bertholle on a French cookbook for American readers. The manuscript went through years of testing, revision, and publishing difficulty before Mastering the Art of French Cooking appeared in 1961. Child then moved into television, where she demonstrated techniques for a mass audience. Her second career became highly influential in American food culture. The transition was gradual and collaborative rather than a single act of reinvention. It shows influence growing through shared work, repeated practice, and the ability to translate expertise from one culture and professional setting into another. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. Line 1 | TW-WL-H33-L1 | XIANG-L-33-02

193爻 Historical event Henry Ford introduces the five-dollar day. Ford Motor Company had introduced moving assembly-line methods that sharply increased automobile production, but repetitive factory work was associated with high employee turnover. Constant hiring and training threatened the efficiency gains of the production system. In 1914 Ford announced a five-dollar daily wage for qualifying workers, far above common factory pay at the time, along with a shorter eight-hour shift. The policy attracted large numbers of applicants and helped stabilize the workforce, though eligibility initially came with intrusive company oversight of workers’ private lives. The wage policy became one of the most famous workplace decisions of the industrial era and was linked to Ford’s ability to operate intensive mass production. It also shows the limits of a simple “high pay” story: compensation, control, productivity, and employee autonomy were intertwined. Great organizational power created the ability to reshape work, but also the responsibility to decide how far employer authority should extend. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. Historical case EUUS-WL-H34: Katherine Johnson accepts aerospace research work · Virginia, United States · 1953 onward

Line 1 | TW-WL-H34-L1 | XIANG-L-34-02

199爻 Historical event Katherine Johnson accepts aerospace research work. Katherine Johnson had trained as a mathematician and worked as a teacher before learning that the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics was hiring women mathematicians. Segregation and gender barriers sharply constrained professional opportunities for Black women in technical fields. She joined the West Area Computing unit at Langley in 1953 and later moved into flight research. Johnson calculated and checked trajectories for early U.S. space missions, including work connected with John Glenn’s orbital flight and later Apollo missions. Her role grew as she asked to attend technical briefings and contribute directly to analytical work that had often been separated by job classification. Johnson spent decades at NASA and became widely recognized much later in life for work that had previously been less visible to the public. The career demonstrates progress through both skill and institutional access: advancement can require not only doing excellent work, but also gaining entry to the rooms where decisions are made. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. Historical case EUUS-WL-H35: Oskar Schindler redirects his factory to protect workers · Occupied Poland and Czechoslovakia, Europe · 1939–1945

Line 1 | TW-WL-H35-L1 | XIANG-L-35-02▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H35-L1 | XIANG-L-35-02

205爻 Historical event Oskar Schindler redirects his factory to protect workers. Oskar Schindler was a German businessman who acquired an enamelware factory in occupied Kraków during the Second World War and initially benefited from the wartime economy and the exploitation surrounding forced labor. As Nazi persecution intensified, he used his factory, contacts, bribes, and claims about essential war production to protect Jewish workers from deportation. In 1944 he moved many workers to a new factory at Brünnlitz in the Sudetenland, where they survived until the end of the war. The records include the well-known lists connected with those transfers. More than a thousand Jews associated with his factories survived. Schindler’s postwar business ventures were not notably successful, and he was later recognized by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations. The case involves an ethically complex transformation in the use of a workplace: an enterprise that began within an exploitative system became a means of sheltering people from it. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The record does not require invented dialogue or private motives to make the decision understandable. It can be followed through observable actions, roles, projects, and later consequences. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. What matters historically is the chain from the conditions before the choice, through the work required to carry it out, to the consequences that became visible afterward. Later reputation can make the result look obvious, but it was not obvious at the beginning. The value of the episode lies in the documented sequence of action and consequence, not in turning the person into a flawless model.

210爻 Historical event Oskar Schindler redirects his factory to protect workers. Oskar Schindler was a German businessman who acquired an enamelware factory in occupied Kraków during the Second World War and initially benefited from the wartime economy and the exploitation surrounding forced labor. As Nazi persecution intensified, he used his factory, contacts, bribes, and claims about essential war production to protect Jewish workers from deportation. In 1944 he moved many workers to a new factory at Brünnlitz in the Sudetenland, where they survived until the end of the war. The records include the well-known lists connected with those transfers. More than a thousand Jews associated with his factories survived. Schindler’s postwar business ventures were not notably successful, and he was later recognized by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations. The case involves an ethically complex transformation in the use of a workplace: an enterprise that began within an exploitative system became a means of sheltering people from it. 211爻 Historical event Eleanor Roosevelt builds an independent public role. Eleanor Roosevelt’s public life developed within a prominent political family, but she gradually built activities that were not reducible to her husband Franklin Roosevelt’s career. She taught, worked with reform organizations, wrote, and developed political networks before becoming first lady. In the White House she traveled extensively, held women-only press conferences, wrote a syndicated column, and reported on social and labor conditions. After Franklin Roosevelt’s death she continued public work, serving as a U.S. delegate to the United Nations and chairing the committee involved in drafting the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Her long career shows a household and professional decision intertwined: family position created obligations and access, but she developed a separate working identity through repeated public responsibilities. Line 1 | TW-WL-H37-L1 | XIANG-L-37-02

217爻 Historical event Rachel Carson publishes Silent Spring. Rachel Carson had worked as a marine biologist and writer for the U.S. government and had already published successful books about the sea. By the late 1950s she began investigating the environmental effects of widespread pesticide use, especially DDT. She gathered scientific studies, consulted researchers, and developed the material into Silent Spring. The book appeared first in serialized form and then as a book in 1962. Chemical-industry organizations and some scientists attacked its arguments, while other scientists and public officials treated the concerns as serious enough for investigation and policy debate. Silent Spring became a major influence on modern environmental awareness and pesticide regulation. Carson died in 1964, before many later policy changes. The case shows a professional decision to publish a contested conclusion when the evidence led away from established industrial practice, accepting that disagreement would follow rather than waiting for universal approval. 220爻 Historical event Rachel Carson publishes Silent Spring. Rachel Carson had worked as a marine biologist and writer for the U.S. government and had already published successful books about the sea. By the late 1950s she began investigating the environmental effects of widespread pesticide use, especially DDT. She gathered scientific studies, consulted researchers, and developed the material into Silent Spring. The book appeared first in serialized form and then as a book in 1962. Chemical-industry organizations and some scientists attacked its arguments, while other scientists and public officials treated the concerns as serious enough for investigation and policy debate. Silent Spring became a major influence on modern environmental awareness and pesticide regulation. Carson died in 1964, before many later policy changes. The case shows a professional decision to publish a contested conclusion when the evidence led away from established industrial practice, accepting that disagreement would follow rather than waiting for universal approval. Line 1 | TW-WL-H38-L1 | XIANG-L-38-02▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H38-L1 | XIANG-L-38-02

223爻 Historical event Ludwig van Beethoven continues composing after severe hearing loss. Beethoven built his career as a pianist and composer in Vienna, but his hearing deteriorated while he was still relatively young. For a professional musician, the loss threatened both public performance and ordinary communication. He reduced his performing career but continued composing, increasingly relying on written conversation and his internal knowledge of musical structure. Major works from his later years included symphonies, piano sonatas, string quartets, and the Missa solemnis. His working methods adapted around the disability rather than restoring the earlier conditions of his career. Beethoven died in 1827 with a body of late work that became central to the classical repertoire. The story is not one of “overcoming” a disability as if the loss were unimportant. It is a practical example of redesigning work when a core ability changes: reducing some activities, relying more heavily on others, and preserving the part of the vocation that remained possible. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. Line 1 | TW-WL-H39-L1 | XIANG-L-39-02

229爻 Historical event Patagonia transfers ownership to mission-focused entities. Patagonia grew from a climbing-equipment business associated with Yvon Chouinard into a global outdoor-apparel company with a long record of environmental advocacy. By the 2010s the question of succession and ownership had become important because the company’s value and influence extended beyond its founder. In 2022 the Chouinard family transferred voting stock to the Patagonia Purpose Trust and nonvoting stock to the Holdfast Collective, a nonprofit organized to use distributions for environmental purposes. The company continued operating as a for-profit business, but the ownership structure was redesigned so that control and economic benefits were directed toward stated long-term goals. The arrangement attracted praise and scrutiny over governance, taxes, and accountability. Whatever view one takes of the structure, it represents a deliberate decrease in conventional family ownership rights in exchange for a mission-oriented succession plan. The life decision concerned what to give up in order to preserve a chosen purpose after the founder’s active role. 235爻 Historical event Sara Blakely starts Spanx while keeping her day job. Sara Blakely was selling fax machines door to door when she began developing an idea for footless shaping hosiery. She had limited experience in apparel manufacturing and did not initially leave her paid job to pursue the idea full-time. She researched patents, contacted hosiery manufacturers, developed prototypes, and used personal savings rather than outside venture capital. After finding a manufacturer willing to produce the product, she worked on packaging and retail outreach. Spanx launched in 2000 and gained national distribution after early retail success and publicity. Blakely later became a prominent entrepreneur and sold a majority stake in Spanx to Blackstone in 2021 while remaining involved. The early sequence shows increase built through bounded risk: the project advanced before the founder abandoned all income and before the market had validated the concept. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. What matters historically is the chain from the conditions before the choice, through the work required to carry it out, to the consequences that became visible afterward. Their roles and ownership evolved as the company expanded and as Allen later stepped back because of illness. Microsoft became one of the world’s largest technology companies. 253爻 Historical event Pixar organizes a collaborative story process. Pixar began as a computer-graphics technology company and gradually shifted toward making animated feature films. Producing a film required artists, writers, engineers, directors, editors, and executives to coordinate over several years. As the studio developed movies such as Toy Story, it built practices for repeated internal review, candid feedback, and revision. The group later known as the “Braintrust” became one visible expression of a broader culture in which work-in-progress could be criticized by peers without transferring formal control of the project away from its director. Pixar produced a long run of commercially successful films and became part of Disney in 2006. Like all creative organizations, it also faced management and cultural challenges. The relevant workplace decision is structural: gathering talented people is not enough; the organization must create a process through which they can improve one another’s work without turning feedback into ownership competition. Line 1 | TW-WL-H44-L1 | XIANG-L-44-02

259爻 Historical event Ursula Burns rises through Xerox and becomes CEO. Ursula Burns joined Xerox as a mechanical-engineering intern in 1980 while completing graduate study. She entered a large technology company at a time when leadership ranks in major U.S. corporations included very few Black women. Burns moved through engineering, product development, operations, and senior management roles. She worked with successive chief executives, took responsibility for major business units, and became president of Xerox before being named chief executive in 2009. Her promotion made her the first Black woman to lead a Fortune 500 company. As CEO she oversaw a major services acquisition and later changes in company structure before stepping down in 2016. Her career illustrates ascent as a sequence rather than a sudden appointment. Technical work, line responsibility, sponsorship, and exposure to different parts of the business accumulated until the organization could evaluate her for enterprise leadership. 265爻 Historical event Oprah Winfrey moves from Baltimore television to Chicago. Oprah Winfrey began working in radio and television news while still young and became an anchor in Baltimore. The fit with conventional evening-news presentation was poor, and she was moved from the anchor desk into a daytime talk format. That change led her toward a style of interviewing and audience interaction that suited her abilities more closely. In 1984 she moved to Chicago to host AM Chicago, which quickly improved its ratings. The program was expanded and renamed The Oprah Winfrey Show, becoming nationally syndicated in 1986. Winfrey later built a media company, production business, magazine, and television network. The career path shows constraint turning into redirection: a setback in one professional format became the occasion to identify a different format in which the same communication skills were more effective. The later success does not make the early dismissal pleasant, but it changed the meaning of the next decision. Historical case EUUS-WL-H46: Mayo Clinic develops a group-practice model · Minnesota, United States · late 1800s–1900s

Line 1 | TW-WL-H46-L1 | XIANG-L-46-02

271爻 Historical event Mayo Clinic develops a group-practice model. William Worrall Mayo and his sons William and Charles developed a medical practice in Rochester, Minnesota, that grew after collaboration with other physicians and with the Sisters of Saint Francis following the 1883 tornado. As patient volume and medical complexity increased, the practice recruited specialists and organized care around shared records, laboratories, salaried physicians, and consultation across disciplines. The model differed from a solo-practice arrangement in which one physician tried to own every part of diagnosis and treatment. The Mayo Clinic became a major medical and research institution. Its history includes many later expansions, but the early organizational decision is clear: expertise was treated as a common resource that could be drawn upon by teams. The “well” in this workplace story is not one star physician; it is the institutional system that makes accumulated knowledge available to patients and colleagues. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. Historical case EUUS-WL-H47: Netflix shifts from DVDs to streaming · United States · 2007 onward

Line 1 | TW-WL-H47-L1 | XIANG-L-47-02▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H47-L1 | XIANG-L-47-02

277爻 Historical event Netflix shifts from DVDs to streaming. Netflix began as a DVD-by-mail rental service and built its early business around subscriptions, logistics, and a large physical catalog. Improvements in broadband created a path for video delivery that could eventually reduce the need to mail discs. In 2007 Netflix introduced streaming for subscribers and gradually invested more heavily in the new mode of delivery. The transition required licensing, software, devices, data infrastructure, and eventually original programming. In 2011 a poorly received attempt to separate the DVD business under the name Qwikster was quickly reversed after customer backlash. Streaming ultimately became the center of Netflix’s business while the DVD service was wound down years later. The case is a workplace transformation rather than a clean one-time pivot: the company had to change technology, contracts, skills, and customer habits while still operating the old model. Some experiments worked; others were reversed. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. 282爻 Historical event Netflix shifts from DVDs to streaming. Netflix began as a DVD-by-mail rental service and built its early business around subscriptions, logistics, and a large physical catalog. Improvements in broadband created a path for video delivery that could eventually reduce the need to mail discs. In 2007 Netflix introduced streaming for subscribers and gradually invested more heavily in the new mode of delivery. The transition required licensing, software, devices, data infrastructure, and eventually original programming. In 2011 a poorly received attempt to separate the DVD business under the name Qwikster was quickly reversed after customer backlash. Streaming ultimately became the center of Netflix’s business while the DVD service was wound down years later. The case is a workplace transformation rather than a clean one-time pivot: the company had to change technology, contracts, skills, and customer habits while still operating the old model. Some experiments worked; others were reversed. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. 283爻 Historical event Alfred Nobel creates the Nobel Prizes through his will. Alfred Nobel became wealthy through inventions, patents, and businesses connected with explosives and industrial technology. By the 1890s he had accumulated a large estate spread across several countries. In 1895 he signed a will directing most of his fortune into a fund whose investment income would support annual prizes in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature, and peace. The instructions surprised some relatives and required years of legal and organizational work after his death in 1896. The Nobel Foundation was established to administer the assets and prizes. The first prizes were awarded in 1901, creating an institution that continued far beyond Nobel’s own business career. The decision transformed private wealth into a recurring public process with rules, committees, investment management, and international recognition. The “cauldron” is institutional: resources are converted into a different form of value through a durable container. Historical case EUUS-WL-H49: Johnson Space Center responds to the Challenger disaster · United States · 1986 onward

Line 1 | TW-WL-H49-L1 | XIANG-L-49-02▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H49-L1 | XIANG-L-49-02

289爻 Historical event Johnson Space Center responds to the Challenger disaster. The Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart shortly after launch on January 28, 1986, killing all seven crew members. The disaster shocked NASA and halted the shuttle program while investigators examined technical and organizational causes. The Rogers Commission identified the failure of an O-ring seal in unusually cold conditions and criticized decision processes surrounding the launch. NASA redesigned solid rocket booster joints, changed management and safety practices, and did not resume shuttle flights until 1988. The return to flight came after testing, review, and organizational changes rather than a rapid attempt to restore the schedule. The Challenger case remains a central example in engineering ethics and organizational communication because warnings, hierarchy, schedule pressure, and technical uncertainty interacted. Shock was not itself a lesson; the lesson depended on whether the institution preserved evidence and changed the system that had produced the decision. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. 295爻 Historical event Bill Watterson ends Calvin and Hobbes. Bill Watterson’s Calvin and Hobbes became one of the most widely read newspaper comic strips of its era. Its success created strong demand for licensing, merchandising, and continued publication. Watterson resisted most merchandising and fought for greater control over page layout and artistic presentation. In 1995 he announced that he would end the strip at the end of the year, despite its popularity and commercial value. The final installment appeared on December 31, 1995. Watterson largely withdrew from the public commercial comics industry afterward and pursued private artistic interests. The decision demonstrates keeping still as a career choice: stopping can be intentional when continuing would require compromises the creator does not want to make. It also shows that the market’s willingness to buy more does not create an obligation to produce more. 301爻 Historical event Vera Wang shifts from skating and publishing to fashion. Vera Wang trained seriously as a figure skater and competed at a high level, but she did not make the U.S. Olympic team. She then moved into fashion publishing and spent many years at Vogue before working at Ralph Lauren. When planning her own wedding, she became dissatisfied with available bridal options and eventually entered bridal design. In 1990 she opened a bridal boutique in New York, first carrying established designers and then developing her own collections. The business expanded into a global fashion brand. The path was gradual and built on skills from earlier stages: discipline from sport, visual judgment from editorial work, and industry knowledge from fashion companies. The case shows that a career change does not have to discard previous identities. Progress can be sequential, with each stage supplying capabilities that make the next stage more credible. 307爻 Historical event Martha Stewart turns a catering business into a media career. Martha Stewart worked in modeling and then as a stockbroker before moving with her family to Connecticut. She developed skills in cooking, entertaining, gardening, and home renovation while building a local catering business. The catering work led to publishing opportunities. Her first book, Entertaining, appeared in 1982, followed by additional books, television appearances, a magazine, and eventually Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia. The business connected practical domestic activities with publishing, retail, licensing, and broadcast media. Her later career included serious legal and corporate setbacks, followed by continued business activity after imprisonment. The earlier transition is useful as a life-and-work case because it turned activities often treated as private household labor into a structured professional platform. The new career emerged from a different status relationship than her earlier finance job and required redefining what counted as marketable expertise. 319爻 Historical event Mark Twain leaves riverboating and builds a writing career. Samuel Clemens trained and worked as a Mississippi River pilot before the American Civil War disrupted commercial river traffic. The occupation had required technical knowledge, navigation, and a specific regional economy. He traveled west, tried mining, worked in journalism, and began publishing humorous sketches under the name Mark Twain. Reporting assignments and travel supplied material for books, and his lecture career added another source of income and public visibility. Writing gradually replaced his earlier occupational identity. Twain became one of the best-known American authors, but he also experienced business failures and financial problems later in life. Line 1 | TW-WL-H55-L1 | XIANG-L-55-02 | Record 325▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H55-L1 | XIANG-L-55-02 | Record 325

325爻 Historical event IKEA standardizes flat-pack furniture. Ingvar Kamprad founded IKEA in Sweden as a mail-order business and gradually focused it on furniture. Shipping assembled furniture was expensive and vulnerable to damage, limiting how efficiently products could reach customers. During the 1950s IKEA increasingly adopted flat-pack designs that customers could transport and assemble themselves. Designers worked within constraints of packaging, manufacturing, cost, and simple assembly. The company paired this with catalogs, large self-service stores, standardized product names, and a retail experience that explained the system to customers. The model expanded internationally and became closely associated with IKEA’s identity. Its influence was not based on one dramatic invention but on persistent design decisions that penetrated many parts of the business. Small operational choices reinforced one another until the whole customer experience worked differently. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. Historical case EUUS-WL-H56: LEGO returns to its core building system · Denmark, Europe · 2004 onward

Line 1 | TW-WL-H56-L1 | XIANG-L-56-02 | Record 331▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H56-L1 | XIANG-L-56-02 | Record 331

331爻 Historical event LEGO returns to its core building system. LEGO entered the early 2000s with declining financial performance after expanding into many products and ventures beyond its traditional construction toys. Complexity increased across themes, components, licensing, and operations. In 2004 Jørgen Vig Knudstorp became chief executive. The company sold or reduced some peripheral activities, simplified operations, improved control of costs and inventory, and refocused attention on the core brick system while still developing licensed and digital products. Product teams were pushed to understand profitability as well as creativity. LEGO returned to strong growth and became one of the world’s largest toy companies. The turnaround did not mean rejecting innovation; it meant reconnecting new ideas to a coherent foundation. Joy in the product became economically sustainable when the organization restored discipline around what it was uniquely good at. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. 337爻 Historical event Automattic builds a distributed company. Automattic was founded around WordPress-related products and from an early stage hired people who worked from many locations rather than from a single headquarters. Distributed work was unusual for a growing technology company in the mid-2000s. The company developed written communication practices, online collaboration tools, periodic in-person gatherings, and hiring processes designed for remote work. Employees could live in different countries and time zones, which broadened recruiting but also increased the need for documentation and asynchronous coordination. Automattic grew into a large distributed organization and became a frequently cited example of remote-first work. The model is not free of tradeoffs; it requires deliberate communication and can make informal coordination harder. The case illustrates dispersion managed through common systems rather than through physical proximity. Historical case EUUS-WL-H58: Basecamp formalizes a forty-hour workweek culture · United States · 2000s–2010s

Line 1 | TW-WL-H58-L1 | XIANG-L-58-02 | Record 343▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H58-L1 | XIANG-L-58-02 | Record 343

343爻 Historical event Basecamp formalizes a forty-hour workweek culture. The software company 37signals, later known as Basecamp, built products with a relatively small team and publicly argued against the idea that long hours were a necessary sign of commitment in technology work. Its leaders wrote about limiting meetings, reducing simultaneous projects, using fixed cycles, and maintaining roughly forty-hour workweeks, with shorter weeks in some summer periods. These practices were tied to product choices that favored smaller teams and limited scope rather than constant expansion. The company remained private and profitable for many years, though its culture and policies also became controversial during later internal disputes. The workplace decision is about limitation: a boundary around hours and project load can support focus, but only if the organization also limits what it promises customers and itself. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. Line 1 | TW-WL-H59-L1 | XIANG-L-59-02 | Record 349▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H59-L1 | XIANG-L-59-02 | Record 349

349爻 Historical event Cadbury develops Bournville as a worker community. Cadbury expanded chocolate manufacturing near Birmingham during the nineteenth century. As the business grew, George and Richard Cadbury moved production to a less crowded site at Bournville, where there was room for a larger factory and a different environment around it. The company and related trusts developed housing, green space, recreation, and community facilities for workers and residents. The model reflected Quaker social ideas as well as practical concerns about health, stability, and the conditions of industrial employment. It was still a company-centered environment, and later observers have debated the balance between welfare and paternalism. Bournville influenced discussions of model villages and employer responsibility. The case is useful for inner truth because stated values were made visible in physical investment. Credibility depended on whether workers could experience the policy in housing, sanitation, recreation, and workplace conditions rather than only in company language. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. Line 1 | TW-WL-H61-L1 | XIANG-L-61-02 | Record 361

361爻 Historical event Apollo 11 team returns from the Moon and shifts to follow-on work. Apollo 11 achieved the first crewed lunar landing in July 1969 after years of engineering, testing, accidents, budget commitments, and work by a very large NASA and contractor workforce. The landing fulfilled the central public objective set for the Apollo program earlier in the decade. After the mission, Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, Michael Collins, flight controllers, engineers, and managers moved into different assignments. NASA still had additional Apollo missions, scientific goals, hardware decisions, and institutional questions to manage. The achievement did not eliminate risk, as later missions such as Apollo 13 demonstrated. Apollo 11 became a symbol of completion, but the program’s work continued and eventually ended after Apollo 17 in 1972. The case illustrates a common workplace problem after success: a milestone can create the illusion that the system no longer needs vigilance. Completion changes the task; it does not abolish the need for maintenance, learning, and decisions about what comes next. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The record does not require invented dialogue or private motives to make the decision understandable. It can be followed through observable actions, roles, projects, and later consequences. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. Line 1 | TW-WL-H64-L1 | XIANG-L-64-02 | Record 379

379爻 Historical event Tim Berners-Lee helps keep the World Wide Web open. Tim Berners-Lee worked at CERN, where researchers needed better ways to share information across different computers and institutions. In 1989 he proposed a hypertext system that became the foundation of the World Wide Web. He developed core technologies including HTML, HTTP, and the first web server and browser. CERN later released the web software into the public domain, allowing others to build compatible sites and tools without paying licensing fees. Berners-Lee then moved to MIT and founded the World Wide Web Consortium to coordinate open standards. The web expanded far beyond the environment in which it was created and became basic infrastructure for communication, commerce, publishing, and software. The decision to support open standards did not settle every later problem of privacy, competition, or platform power. It left the system deliberately unfinished so that others could extend it. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The record does not require invented dialogue or private motives to make the decision understandable. It can be followed through observable actions, roles, projects, and later consequences. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. What matters historically is the chain from the conditions before the choice, through the work required to carry it out, to the consequences that became visible afterward. Later reputation can make the result look obvious, but it was not obvious at the beginning. The value of the episode lies in the documented sequence of action and consequence, not in turning the person into a flawless model.
